claims.text: Retention of toughness in refractory high-entropy alloys is governed by the synergistic effects of local lattice distortion and high grain-boundary density.
Local lattice distortion creates a rough or complex energy landscape.
The complex energy landscape equalizes the mobilities of vacancies and interstitials.
Similar vacancy and interstitial mobilities enhance defect recombination.
A high density of grain boundaries provides sites that aid defect recombination.
Enhanced recombination suppresses damage sites such as irradiation-induced dislocation loops and microcrack precursors.
The studied as-deposited W-Ta-V-Cr alloy has a bimodal microstructure in which approximately 70% of grains are no larger than 100 nm.
The studied alloy was produced by magnetron sputtering deposition.
Thermal annealing can be used as a controlled intervention intended to increase average grain size beyond 500 nm while retaining overall alloy composition.
The relevant comparison can be conducted under irradiation temperatures up to 1073 K and moderate-to-high displacement doses.
Increasing grain size reduces grain-boundary density.
Reduced grain-boundary density permits greater defect accumulation.
Greater defect accumulation caused by grain growth leads to loss of toughness.
Relative to the nanocrystalline baseline, the annealed larger-grained alloy will exhibit increased defect clustering.
Relative to the nanocrystalline baseline, the annealed larger-grained alloy will exhibit lower toughness retention and reduced resistance to crack initiation or propagation.
No irradiation-created dislocation loops were observed in the studied nanocrystalline alloy after irradiation to 8 dpa at 1073 K.
The nanocrystalline baseline exhibits balanced defect mobilities and high toughness retention under irradiation.
The proposed governing behavior may not apply to bulk alloys or to high-entropy alloys with substantially different compositions or microstructures.
